This is consequential: it places BEHENTRIMONIUM CHLORIDE @12, the formula's ONLY cationic surfactant, in the tail, leaving the credited segment with no cationic conditioning agent at all. No §3.1 anomaly by the letter (rank 11 > 3, and Cetearyl Alcohol @3 is a conditioning ingredient preceding the marker), but see AP-06-NOCATIONIC.

weightPotential.evidenceScope: Formula-only, above-tail ranks 1–10; an ingredient-informed matching prior, not a prediction of visible flattening.
weightPotential.rationale: This is the cohort's most obviously heavy formula on the face of it — a dimethicone/dimethiconol pair plus a shea butter plus three plant oils, all above the marker — and it lands on `moderate`, because §9.2's `high` anchor requires a REQUIRED BASE of two distinct cationics above the tail, and this formula has none. Both `low` conjuncts also fail. `moderate` is what the anchor structure leaves. E2 ceiling: weight deposition potential, never measured finish.

weightPotential.derivation: §9.2 `high` = required base (≥2 distinct cationics above the tail AND a cetearyl-class fatty alcohol in the top three) PLUS at least one of (a) R4b heavy lipid above the tail or (b) an occlusive silicone stack above the tail. Both supporting alternatives are satisfied — the only cohort product where that is true — but the required base fails on its cationic leg, and the base is required, not optional (Nick's 2026-09-04 ruling: the first two markers are the required base, the last two are alternatives). `low` = single cationic species AND no cetearyl-class fatty alcohol in the top three AND no R4b heavy lipid above the tail: conjuncts 2 and 3 both fail. Residual = `moderate`.
thresholdReasoning: Clears `moderate`: everything the high and low anchors do not capture; §9.2 calls this the expected majority and explicitly accepts it.

`high` does not apply, and this is the cohort's most important weight finding: the anchor's required base is a CONDITIONING-architecture test (cationic breadth plus fatty-alcohol rank) being used as the gate on a WEIGHT value, while the two markers that actually speak to weight — the heavy lipid and the occlusive silicone stack — are demoted to optional alternatives. A formula can satisfy both weight-relevant markers and still be refused `high`, which is what happened here. See AP-06-WEIGHTGATE.
`low` does not apply: Cetearyl Alcohol @3 is in the top three, and shea butter and coconut oil are above the tail.
§9.2 conflict fallback not engaged: no lightness positioning to contradict a `high` that was not reached in any case.
counterSignals: The graded direct property `weight_deposition_potential` reads `higher` while the profile field reads `moderate`. That divergence is not an error in either — it is the anchor's required base doing work the graded property does not — but it is exactly the kind of internal inconsistency a calibration should surface.
'ohne Silikone' claim is contradicted by the formula and was given no weight in either direction (§9.2: silicone-free proves nothing about lightness; silicone presence is not the weight driver).
limitations: A soft preference with a stated reason, never an exclusion.

adjudicationPoints.title: Claims never override formula — the silicone-free case, resolved as designed
adjudicationPoints.body: MONDAY's brand positioning is 'ohne Silikone'. This SKU's confirmed INCI carries Dimethicone @4, Dimethiconol @5 and Amodimethicone @18. The standard handled it correctly and without special-casing: the claim entered none of the five channels §11 step 4 permits, the silicone pair set the primary focus on formula evidence alone, and the claim is recorded as a contradiction in counter_signals. Note also that the brand's own 'versiegelt die Haarkutikula' wording is on §9.5.4's absolute banned list; it is quoted as claim context and adopted nowhere. No rule change is proposed — this is the discrimination logic working, and it should be reported to Nick as a passed stress test rather than a problem.

adjudicationPoints.title: §9.2's `high` weight anchor is gated on a conditioning test, and refuses the cohort's heaviest formula
adjudicationPoints.body: This formula satisfies BOTH of §9.2's weight-relevant supporting alternatives — an R4b heavy lipid above the tail (shea @7, coconut @8) and an occlusive silicone stack above the tail (the named dimethicone/dimethiconol pair @4/@5) — and is still refused `high`, because the required base demands two distinct cationic surfactants above the tail and this formula's single cationic is one rank below the marker. The base is a conditioning-architecture test being used as the gate on a weight value; the markers that actually speak to weight are the optional half. Downstream, this product is offered as a broad prior for fine hair. §18 open question 1 framed the choice as conjunction-versus-alternatives; this cohort shows the sharper question is whether the cationic leg belongs in the weight anchor at all. Candidate fix: make the required base the fatty-alcohol rank alone, and let either weight-relevant alternative complete it; or allow an R4b-plus-silicone-stack double alternative to substitute for the missing cationic leg.
adjudicationPoints.source: §9.2 anchors and Nick's 2026-09-04 ruling; §18 open question 1

adjudicationPoints.title: conditioning_level `high` is reachable with no cationic conditioning agent in the credited segment
adjudicationPoints.body: S2 plus S3 alone reach `high`. Here that means a mask whose only cationic surfactant sits below the tail marker is classified at the top of the conditioning scale on fatty-alcohol rank and lipid breadth. D1's ruled signal families are cationic count and rank, fatty-alcohol rank, and lipid-above-tail breadth — three families, of which the cationic one is arguably the most load-bearing for a lamellar-gel-network category, yet the counting rule lets any two of three carry an extreme. Candidate fix for the calibration review: require S1 to be among the satisfied signals for `high`, or require all three for `high` and treat two as an upper-moderate.
